newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccans give huge "yes" for parliamentary change.
newsitem.headline: Moroccans give huge "yes" for parliamentary change.

text.p: More than 10 million Moroccans voted overwhelmingly for King Hassan's plans to change the constitution and give the country a powerful new upper house of parliament to strengthen regional representation.
Interior ministry final figures early on Saturday showed 99.56 percent, or 10.16 million people, voting "yes" in the Friday referendum, compared with only 45,324 who opposed the reforms.
Total turnout was 82.95 of the 12.3 million electorate, and there were 31,639 spoilt votes.
Pro-government and opposition parties had called for a "yes" vote, but many of those casting their ballots gave their reason as loyalty to King Hassan.
"I voted today to respond to King Hassan's appeal," said Khadija al-Idrissi, a 42-year-old housewife, casting her ballot at the Lycee Hassan II in the capital, Rabat.
The changes to the 1992 constitution will lead to the existing 333-seat parliament being dissolved, and two assemblies formed.
A new lower house, the Majlis Anuwab (Chamber of Representatives), will be directly elected and the new upper assembly, the Majlis al-Mustasharin (Consultative Chamber), indirectly.

Despite its name, the upper house will have power to force a no-confidence vote in the government. Officials say it will also help ensure development in rural areas, home to 50 percent of Morocco's 27 million people, and a major contributor through farm products to foreign currency earnings.
Upper house members will be indirectly elected, mainly through local councils, professional bodies and trade unions.

King Hassan, whose paramount powers will not be touched, cast his vote in Skhirat, 20 km (12 miles) from Rabat, at 3 p.m. (1500 GMT). Wearing a white blazer and green trousers, he waved and smiled to a cheering crowd.

"It's an historic moment for this country. For the first time there is a general consensus, including the opposition, to vote "yes' for the proposals," said one senior official on the eve of the vote.

Morocco's main opposition parties, the old-guard Istiqlal party and Socialist Union of People's Forces (USFP), both of whom have long demand direct elections to parliament, both called for a "yes" vote.

Only small parties called for a boycott or a "no" vote. One, the Avant-Garde Democratic and Socialist Party, said on Friday police had arrested 10 of its members while they were campaigning on Thursday for a boycott of the referendum. An interior ministry official said he was not aware of the arrests.
